analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate prices directly with drugmakers for brand-name drugs with no generic competition.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in two House committees from December 2015 until the Congress ended in January 2017, and current law still bars Medicare from negotiating drug prices.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, Medicare is explicitly forbidden from negotiating drug prices with manufacturers; the government pays whatever private plans manage to bargain for. This bill would carve out an exception for brand-name drugs that face no competition — single-source drugs and biologics — and require the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate a maximum price for them. If talks fail after 90 days, the Secretary could set the price based on the manufacturer's costs and prices paid by the VA and Medicaid, with increases in later years capped at inflation. Manufacturers would have to participate as a condition of selling into Medicare.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare's roughly 40 million drug-benefit enrollees, who pay premiums and out-of-pocket costs tied to drug prices, and taxpayers, who help fund the program. Anyone whose pharmacy bill reflects the price of brand-name drugs with no generic rival stands to pay less if negotiation brings prices down.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate the price that may be charged for specified single-source drugs and biologics — brand-name drugs with no generic competition — for Medicare's prescription drug benefit [S2].

If the manufacturer and the Secretary cannot agree on a price within 90 days, the Secretary sets a maximum price based on the manufacturer's cost information, the net price paid by the VA or Medicaid, and affordability for beneficiaries [S3].

Price increases in later years are capped at the consumer price index, and manufacturers must participate in negotiation as a condition of having their drugs covered under the Medicare drug benefit [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose Medicare revenue on non-competed drugs would be capped at the negotiated or Secretary-set maximum price, and whose pricing strategy under Medicare would no longer be whatever the market bears.

drawbacks.text: If negotiations fail, the fallback lets the Secretary set a price from manufacturer cost data and other programs' prices — a government-set price that manufacturers argue could be set too low to fund research on future drugs [S3].
The bill covers only single-source drugs and biologics, not the broader drug market, so most drugs would remain priced through the existing system of private plan negotiations [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large: prescription drugs are one of the fastest-growing costs in Medicare, and the bill targets the segment — brand-name drugs without competition — where purchasers have the least bargaining power. The main cost falls on drug manufacturers, not on beneficiaries or taxpayers. The honest trade-off is that government-set prices can under-reward future drug development if set too aggressively, and the bill's scope is narrower than full Medicare price negotiation.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and their Health subcommittee on the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever took it up before the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on December 9, 2015, joined by seven original cosponsors [S3].
It had 10 cosponsors by the end, all Democrats [S4].

The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and then to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee; the record shows no hearing, markup, or floor action afterward [S5].
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and all bills not passed die with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: the current-law ban on Medicare price negotiation stayed in place, so their pricing on non-competed drugs remained unrestricted. Medicare beneficiaries kept paying prices set without government bargaining.

for.name: Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 10 cosponsors, all fellow Democrats

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and referred it to its Health Subcommittee; never scheduled a hearing or markup

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral; never took it up

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Brand-name drug manufacturers and their trade association
against.what_they_did: Long opposed letting the government negotiate Medicare drug prices, defending the noninterference clause this bill would have repealed

sides.party_line_note: All 11 supporters — the sponsor and 10 cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican signed on [S4].

industries.note: The bill would cap the price these companies can charge Medicare for drugs with no generic or biosimilar competition, ending the current-law rule that keeps the government out of price-setting. Manufacturers lose revenue on exactly the drugs where they now face no bargaining pressure.

industries.industry: Medicare prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage insurers
industries.note: The negotiated maximum price applies to what these plans pay for specified drugs, lowering their drug costs, while the bill leaves plan formulary rules untouched [S2]. They gain on drug costs but keep their role as the purchasing channel.
